newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's transition process thrown into doubt.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's transition process thrown into doubt.

text.p: Ecuador faced new political uncertainty on Monday because interim President Rosalia Arteaga raised doubts about a military-backed deal to hand over power to the head of Congress as early as Tuesday.

Arteaga was appointed head of a caretaker government on Sunday as part of an agreement between lawmakers and the armed forces to end the crisis that erupted on Thursday when flamboyant populist President Abdala Bucaram was ousted by a divided Congress on grounds of "mental incompetence."

Congressional sources said the deal was based on the understanding that Arteaga would step down within a few days, once legislation was approved allowing congressional leader Fabian Alarcon to be appointed interim head of state.

Alarcon, who would retain Arteaga as vice president, would serve until a new, democratically elected president was sworn in on Aug. 10, 1998. But Arteaga, a 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister, threw cold water on the "transition deal" in a news conference at the presidential palace on Sunday.

Sounding somewhat like Bucaram himself -- the man called "El Loco" who dubbed his ouster a "congressional coup" that violated the constitution -- she said Alarcon would be unable to assume the presidency until constitutional reforms were approved allowing Congress to appoint a president.

Such reforms require more than two-thirds of the 82-member Congress, and Alarcon, the only likely candidate, could have a difficult time mustering the necessary votes. This is especially true if Bucaram, who was rumoured to be planning to hand over to Arteaga after his ouster by 44-34 votes on Thursday night, works to block Alarcon's bid for power.
Alarcon was initially voted in as president by Congress on Thursday after two days of demonstrations protesting Bucaram's austerity plan had paralysed the country.

Bucaram left the capital late on Friday and gave up his fight for the presidency on Sunday after the military withdrew its support. But he remained defiant, vowing to try again for the presidency of the Andean nation of 12 million people.
The accord that paved the way for Alarcon to succeed Arteaga specifies that he could be appointed by a simple majority. But Arteaga said the deal was legally flawed.

"Under the current constitution, Congress does not have the capacity to designate a president," she said. "Congress, in which we trust, must therefore find the legal channels and enact the pertinent reforms in order to proceed."
She stressed that she intended to remain in office "as long as necessary to restore democratic order."

Clearly angered by her comments, Alarcon said Arteaga -- who spoke ambitiously about the direction economic and social policy would take under her government -- appeared to be suffering from delusions of grandeur.
"I can't believe this," he said. "She spoke about macroeconomic policies that will only last three days, and foreign policy for the next three days."

"No (constitutional) reforms will be dealt with on Tuesday, no reforms are needed," he added. "The only thing that will be dealt with tomorrow is the designation of the interim president of the republic."
Arteaga had no immediate response to Alarcon's challenge of her authority to interpret the constitution. But former President Leon Febres Cordero sided squarely with Alarcon.
"It looks as though it's going to be necessary to give Mrs. Rosalia Arteaga a delicate pull by the ears to get her out of the presidency no later than Tuesday," he told a television interviewer.

The military, the ultimate power-brokers, have yet to comment on the standoff between Arteaga and Alarcon. But they pledged "absolute respect for the constitution" in a statement issued shortly before Arteaga's news conference on Sunday.
The extraordinary session of Congress, in which Alarcon said he will be duly appointed president, was set for 4 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Tuesday.
